AI video 101:  edit images & create video
A class taught with One Club for Creativity in San Diego. Step by step tutorial to become a superhero.

Want to get up to  speed on character creation and video generation? This tutorial is beginer friendly. From image generation to video generation. We put it together with Robbie Norris and Jon Merlin for an in person at The One Club for Creativity. At One Clubs AI video 101, the goal was to help you turn yourself into a superhero, and fly around an imaginary scene. We included cinematic approaches, because knowledge of realism works for many applications. Tho personal its not really my own jam - I like to change the style away from realism.
You can find the presentation [here](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/17TI9xlXfJ7_4ypRb5JS6_SuGOacQlbVjslPAwAt3UMk/edit?slide=id.g3f58a166942_0_13#slide=id.g3f58a166942_0_13). And I'll walk you though the process below, step by step, with links.
![](/src/assets/blogs/ai-video-101-how-to-edit-images-and-create-video-step-by-step-tutorial-to-become-a-superhero-inline-1.png)
You need an image of yourself to start a transform. From the browser window click the share icon (1) in the upper right to show the QR code for the specific page you are working on. Scan it with your phone to capture references of yourself (or a location, or pose, or object, etc). From a technical perspective you can work with any image. Using your own likeness requires the least amount of consent or risk of takedown. Side note: we recommend using paid APIs to protect your privacy. (All models on 10zebra are paid, and none of the outside model providers run through freemium services) While you may supplement your projects with freemium tools and CPP programs outside of 10zebra, (e.g. by uploading those assets into your project), the terms of these systems are beyond our scope and so we can not provide the same clean chain of title reports for those.
![](/src/assets/blogs/ai-video-101-how-to-edit-images-and-create-video-step-by-step-tutorial-to-become-a-superhero-inline-2.png)
Its common to have a "2nd window" for creating. A scratchpad for your prompt before you commit to it. It might be a google document, like the one from Robbie Norris's class, with examples of tested and vetted JSON prompts. It might be another shot in 10zebra project, where you discovered a great sentence to pin down a visual effect. You can copy that prompt, and modify it for your current needs. Sometimes you may want to use an LLM to create a new detailed JSON prompt.
![](/src/assets/blogs/ai-video-101-how-to-edit-images-and-create-video-step-by-step-tutorial-to-become-a-superhero-inline-3.png)
Iteration is the antidote to slop. Be intentional. If you are building a keyframe for subsequent animation, here are two tips. One: If there is a character that is going to move, capture them in a frozen moment, with the intention of movement (not just standing there idly). Two: (sometimes an opposing goal), If you are going to work a multi shot sequence from an image, try to pack as much information into a core reference: all character and all objects and a relevant location. Then a multishot generation can pull from subsets of that reference. You can also handle this with multiple independent references,  that can be slower and more effortful (say you want to adjust the lighting on all characters)- a strong scene reference can go a long way, and be versatile.
![](/src/assets/blogs/ai-video-101-how-to-edit-images-and-create-video-step-by-step-tutorial-to-become-a-superhero-inline-4.png)
When you have entered your prompt in 10zebra, confirm you are generating a video, and that its the model you want. Our initial defaults strike a balance for quality and cost. We update with all the major model releases. For example: Grok is more cost efficient and Veo tends to be more expensive. At the time of writing this  Sora2 has the highest cost / quality and SeeDance is top performing. Typically you may a just a few words to improve a generation.

What if all that was left to solve on Earth was judgement?
This project puts a contemporary ideology and visual style -  pre-columbian, baroque,  and borderless explorations of a third spaces in the desert - at the heart of a cross cultural narrative. We submit this work as part of the Future Vision XPRIZE competition. We will update this post with more information about the project. In the mean time you may find more information about the art of the De La Torre brothers here: [www.delatorrebrothers.art](https://www.delatorrebrothers.art/) ## LOGLINE After seeing a vengeful criminal hack a doctor's implants and frame a local drifter, two young friends face a deadly choice: keep quiet to survive, or step into an AI-mediated tribunal to speak the truth. ## SYNOPSIS Set in a high-tech desert, this story explores how two friends come of age in a world governed by agentic justice. While hiding out past curfew in the third space between the worlds, they witness a bitter outcast murder a doctor by overriding his heart implant. To cover his tracks, the killer frames Xapawiyeme, an incapacitated drifter, setting her up for permanent Civic Severance. For Huck, survival means staying silent. He knows the killer is a skilled hacker who can use exploits to target them. But Kauyu is consumed by guilt that Xapa’s impending trial would lead to digital exile. In a culture where everyday life and legal systems are mediated by automated agents, the boys face a modern rites-of-passage: learning how to project their own authentic human voice through layers of algorithmic noise. Kauyu realizes that relying on automated feeds without human input allows truth to be manipulated. The Agentic Tribunal scene unfolds as a cross-cultural musical. Kauyu delivers his testimony in a syncopated cumbia rhythm. Blending pre-Columbian motifs, Mexican folklore, and Midwestern American lore, the song weaves together a plot with ancestral lore that transcends national boundaries and time. In this world, the characters—rendered with the luminous, sculpted presence of blown glass—move through a fusion of heritage and high tech, suggesting that moral truth and accountability to your peers will be core to any future society, even if there are many bodies and minds made of fused silica. ## STATEMENT **De La Torre Brothers.**Einar and Jamex De La Torre were born in Guadalajara, México (1963 & 1960). Moving to a California beach town in 1972, the complexities of their bicultural identity and current life on both sides of the border—Baja California and San Diego—deeply inform their practice. Their signature style combines blown glass sculpture, mixed media, and lenticular printing. Their work blends religious iconography, German expressionism, Mexican vernacular arts, and pre-Columbian motifs. They have completed 18 solo museum exhibitions, 8 public art projects, and 4 biennales. **Philip Meier**is a printmaker, neuroscientist, and founder of 10zebra: a next-generation video creation platform. His work centers on visual perception and how artists trick the brain into seeing fiction. Holding a PhD in computational neuroscience from UCSD, he is passionate about drawing, painting, and applying art and science to social problems. Philip helps creative teams blend traditional camera work with generative AI, leveraging curation, reference frameworks, and machine-driven visual understanding to build novel human-machine workflows. **Project Collaboration Statement.**This project is a collaboration between Philip Meier and the De la Torre brothers. The team is pushing into transmedia storytelling. Characters were physically crafted in intricate blown glass by the De la Torre brothers, and then extended into an animated narrative, to create new character variations, and style combinations for this project. After being installed at the Laguna Art Museum for an exhibit of the same name (“The Tipping Point”), every visual asset was captured entirely on a Pixel phone and generated through the 10zebra platform.  Multi-layered worlds—where cumbia, agentic justice, and ancestral memory converge—can be realized dynamically at the edge of mobile technology and collaborative human creativity.  We are fascinated by the labyrinthine complexity our technology promises, and walk forward with curiosity, hoping to help build a better future in this multifaceted world.

Naturally occurring illusions in artificial reality
For your visual system, perception depends on context. For generative AI, it turns out that the context matters a lot as well.

What makes something look bright or dark? You might think that the amount of light coming from a region is what makes something look bright or dark. You would be wrong. It's so much more complicated. And fascinating. Ted Adelson made this image to show you how two patches with the same RGB pixel values can "look" so different.
![](/src/assets/blogs/naturally-occurring-illusions-in-artificial-reality-inline-1.jpg)
The squares with A and B look different colors to us. So what is going on? Context matters. We interpret the shadow. We infer the lighting. We estimate the albedo. Albedo is a fancy word the corresponds to the fraction of light reflected by light. It tends to be used by people who study objects in sky or computer graphics. I think of it as what the paint absorbs in a painting. When you shine a white light on a colorful painting, all that pigment is "removing" a portion of the light, and letting the other part bounce off and hit your eyeball. With gray scale, it's even simpler. So how does this apply to the image. Let's say patch A and B both return a billion photons per millisecond per patch. Thats the same. But if there was more light landing on A, then only a smaller fraction is reflected. Hence it looks dark.
![](/src/assets/blogs/naturally-occurring-illusions-in-artificial-reality-inline-2.jpg)
The Perceptual Science Group at MIT offers this proof and [more](https://persci.mit.edu/gallery/checkershadow/proof). Naturally, I had to think of the checker-shadow illusion when this shadow-stripped zebra visited my genAI artistic explorations. It's also similar to some other illusions that exploit the ambiguous relationship of the meaning of light changes at "x" junctions. (If you are interested in that, Marr's book on Vision is great. Here is a [teaser](https://www.contrib.andrew.cmu.edu/~kk3n/80-300/marr2.pdf)) So the zebra image has all the same ingredients: Patterned black and white albedo, and patterned light. To top it off, the light is moving (but I am not showing that here).
![](/src/assets/blogs/naturally-occurring-illusions-in-artificial-reality-inline-3.jpg)
An image from a video I created yesterday, all with genAI on 10zebra.
![](/src/assets/blogs/naturally-occurring-illusions-in-artificial-reality-inline-4.png)
The patterened light and patterned albedo is similar to the checkershadoow illusion. Does the AI system have a model of reality enough to "know" how light works? Did it get it right? Not quite. Edge statistics influence that output that don't belong in a luminance boundary. Some edges change their type as they extend across space(e.g. an illumination edge, vs. paint edge, vs occlusion) But the generative models, only by working on patches hierarchically, get a lot of the statistic right. Notably these system are also biased system trying to make things that humans find pretty, and that changes something about contrast. But is also captures something about light and motion, esp the parts we like.
![](/src/assets/blogs/naturally-occurring-illusions-in-artificial-reality-inline-5.png)
I added the bar to show how the white stripe in shadow  is close to the dark stripe in full light. Cool. So that just happened. The synthetic checkers on the zebra, I didn't "try to make this illusion." My prompt was "**profile of a zebra walking in an empty white field"**first using one of our new Flux-based systems. And the I reran the result with "Autocine" to get an infinite animated loop. As we pack more data into these generative model, more and more subtle statistics of the world will be trapped in those model weights. Crazy. When I worked with Ted Adelson at MIT I had a weird job. I did research on perceptual illusions made in Flash. But I also maintained the lab's website. That may sound a bit boring, but if you are an art / tech geek like me, it was the bees knees, b/c Ted has one of the coolest websites around. If I could should the "then me" the kind of new magic tech we are brewing, I would be even more stoked. Now, in this modern world of generative ai, everything I learned about perception feels even more relevant. If the pixels themselves are real, then nothing is an illusion. But if you believe the false hood they portray, everything is an illusion.

The result was that I stopped sharing it. Even though I made it for people to see, it somehow seemed tacky. After some time has passed, I still like it, and it makes me smille when I imagine his conversations and the translations for the Italian newspaper. Exactly, thats the view.

You can build them explicitly, and you can even benefit from them in your prompting. So let's take them in order: ### Q1: How do I get cool 3D parallax using just text-to-video? A: Make sure to include objects a three different depth planes. For example include your character, but also say "**soft focus of Martian landscape in the background, dramatic lighting, warm color grade**" for the background, and "***occluded by rock wall in the foreground***" and "**cinematic panning shot with parallax**" You can change the parts, but the components are: something in the background, something in foreground, and some words to describe camera motion that yields parallax, often including the word parallax, or panning motion left or right. This technique is very fast. Its is good for establishing shots, concept pitches, pre-viz and mood boards. Its possible to use these assets in a production using just gen AI, but you should have a plan how to tackle character consistency if re-occurring characters are also in the same environment.
Here is the prompt used for the shot above: **Cinematic panning shot with parallax of a rugged steampunk warrior girl in a leather jacket and dust goggles, occluded by rock wall in the foreground, asymmetric composition, soft focus of Martian landscape in the background, dramatic lighting, warm color grade, cinematic panning shot with parallax, IMAX, 70mm** This was generated on 10zebras platform this morning. (That's October 1st to all you blog readers who don't subscribe). Its worth pointing out, because even if our prompt stratgey may be simiilar, the underlying video models get better over time, with better temporal coherence, and character consistency. Sometimes you fail to get the motion you want, but like the composition. [It is still a genAI model, based on lots of internal noise] In case you want to save the composition, use the "reimagine" button, and simplify your previous prompt. Try including just the camera motion like "pan right." Some of you might we wondering "why not just cut to the chase and give the sample prompt. Why all the 2.5D hacks?" Two reasons. First, I think if you reason about the fundamentals, you can write better prompts and understand why they work and fail. Second, the technical language used by experts gets deeply entwined with how we can prompt to get specific effects. Anyone use :*volumetric lighting:*in thier prompts? Adding a "70mm" still impacts generation, even though their is no actual lens in the diffusion model. So, you will have a much better chance of discovering meaningful prompt improvements by thinking about whats actually gets onto a 2D projection of a camera sensor, human eyeball or virtual camera, and how it gets discussed in production. #### Q2: How do I make assets to create the 2D depth planes? Start with image prompting. Midjourney (closed model) and Flux (open model) are two of your best options at the time of this writing. Try prompting for landscapes isolated from their background, either white or green screen. Yep, you can prompt for a green screen background. This make your comping that much easier. Summarizing the approach above. A strength of -1 lets the intensity map onto depth correctly. The core idea is to use the depth map of a single image to displace the pixels. The fact that this works is similar to why Gaussian splatting works: floating pixels located in 3 space will displace coherently with your camera motion. Of course this basic blender approach lacks all the fancy optimizations the neural nets employ for splatting - all the size color orientation and intensity of each "point" are not adjusted by Blender to be angularly dependent - just the relative position. Ok, not a complete stranger.  I have met James Jones a few times and I have seen his submissions as "Satire AI" through a community we are part of called Machine Cinema. And just last week at a gathering in Los Angeles, I got to know him better. He is an architect with a personal commitment to create videos with AI. Having spent many years abroad in Shanghai, he couldn't shake off the importance of taking off his shoes when entering our host's house.  He pays attention to details. The kind of thoughtful creative I want to empower with AI.
James submitted this time bending work about the historic Huntington hotel as a sample of his work. It's a bit weird - what forces cause this time travel?  Why is she treated by the nurses from an earlier pandemic? The "what if" hypothesis bears fruit. There is a consistency to the visual logic, the pictures on the wall moving, the mixing of realities, the people who move backwards and forward ... I want to know more. I think Satire AI is on to something.  I think James is way more likely than most of us to make something great.  He will push the boundaries and bump into edges, and figure out what works. It's precisely**the impulse to try and explore something new** that aligns with 10zebra.  You need to push on boundaries, and witness failures before you can understand what works. Over the course of a week, we had a few exchanges.  James used the credits I funded him to create a new story, and in exchange he offered helpful feedback about 10zebra.  At the end of the week I saw what he made... It's dark.  Like creepy serial killer dark.  The video shows the first person perspective of someone who has done horrible things. **Ugh, why make content that focuses on death and dismemberment of women?** Don't get me wrong. It's not pure gore.  It is trying to have depth by exploring the motive, and habits, and back story of the murder. I reminded myself that this is not my own work, nor my own voice.  It can be challenging to review content created on your platform and not have a opinion about it. It’s a hard thing to get right and I am striving for it: to think more about the arc of the artist than to judge the specific content. To celebrate the creator and the craft, and to be agnostic about the output.  To provide encouragement on an artistic journey without saying "change this one thing here." I think having a thick skin is important in our polarized world.  As a platform host - I don't want to censor someone's voice because it's not aligned with my own views.  Over the long haul I think protecting his voice under the banner of free speech is more important than the fact that the content is gross or disturbing. But something jumped out at me when reviewing this piece of content. Some people will make content that is even more horrible and more violent than this.  And that is worth unpacking.  I think it's very important that we are not broadsided by content we "don't want to see." Don't get me wrong.  Good art often contains uncomfortable stuff. Greek tragedies are full of horrible stuff, including beheadings.  Tom Huck of Evil Prints can offend people, but his voice adds value to society - even if it is a critique about the downfall of society.  Art Speigelman can address the complexity of the Holocaust in a comic; should we freak out because it falls in the hands of children too early?  As a father of two daughters, I think there is an important differentiation between seeking disturbing content, vs stumbling upon it as part of the fabric of our culture. The conclusion I take is that how you distribute content is a key moment for judgement.  As a society we shouldn't censor ideas at the LLM level, or at the production level.  I think talented artists should have unbridled access to generative models to do as they see fit to express their views and create their art. But we should take care about the distribution of content that impacts us as a society.  And we should hold people accountable for the work that they make.  Sometimes that is simply with our own words in a public forum.  I appreciate James is using his own name and stands behind it along with a collection of his work.  Somehow, the video he made deserves to be appropriately labeled so that it doesn't fall upon the wrong unsuspecting audience.  This used to be covered by movie ratings. Now this effort will fall upon our new distribution channels.  My hunch is that YouTube has the incentive to get this right, but maybe not IG or Tiktok, because the flash in the pan is too fast. I dunno. Do the rewards of shocking content compel someone like James to lean into horrible things to break through the numbing mold of acceptable content? Is it all about shock value? Or is there an underlying message or deeper narrative? I think some kind of video content can create a “collateral damage” to our psyche. I don't think watching creepy content converts us to psychopaths, but I worry that violent and dehumanizing depictions of women dull us, and can lead to normalizing extreme views. Or to living lives with greater fear or greater isolation. But this is not about James’ work, at least not entirely. There is larger societal forces at work here greater than any one single creator. AI, placed in the context of our attention economy, can enable visual media to create rage bate, just like controversial titles in blogs. We have all encountered this in some form - whether in advertisement or politics. I want my community to try hard to set a good example for the next generation of creatives. And it’s not merely attention at any cost. A collection of someone’s work will reveal more about their intentions in the long run. After reflecting on James’ content, including his prior work, I do think he is on to something. I connected with him after viewing his video and he shared some insights about the themes he is exploring, about impulse, about nature and nurture. And I liked his artistic thought process. I liked what he was trying to explore. I just didn’t like some of his choices about how it came across in visual form. James is an artist exploring how he can use new AI tools to create his art. If we start to block his prompts to an LLM, we do a disservice to his artistic process. We don’t allow him to create and explore, we pass judgement that “this isn’t acceptable” without understanding the final product or means of distribution. Horror and thrillers are legitimate categories of creation. They might not be for everyone, but should we police the creation of a story that we personally find disturbing? That is one step away from policing creation based on beliefs or ideology. And I want 10zebra to be a flexible and trustworthy scratchpad for visual thought. But you can’t and shouldn’t police thought. So where does that leave us? I support James. I won't post his full video on our social channels, because I don't believe it belongs there.  I have only included some of his previous work on this blog, not the stuff he made on 10zebra.
